accepted.question_text: For the second-order rational difference equation x_{n+1} = (a + b x_n + g x_{n-1})/(A + B x_n + C x_{n-1}), with nonnegative parameters and positive initial conditions for which the denominator is always positive, prove or disprove that local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium implies global attractivity of that equilibrium. Equivalently, for the first-order planar system x_{n+1} = (a + b x_n + g y_n)/(A + B x_n + C y_n), y_{n+1} = x_n, under the same nonnegative-parameter and positive-initial-condition assumptions, determine whether local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium implies global attractivity.

accepted.question_text: Extend and generalize to planar rational systems the boundedness and convergence trichotomy known for x_{n+1} = (a + b x_n + g x_{n-1})/(A + B x_n + C x_{n-1}), with nonnegative parameters and positive denominators: if C > 0 then every solution is bounded; if C = 0 and B > 0, every solution is bounded exactly when g <= b + A; when g = b + A every solution converges to a not necessarily prime period-two solution; and when g < b + A every solution has a finite limit. The problem is to find the corresponding planar-system generalization, including the right hypotheses and alternatives.

accepted.question_text: For the planar rational system x_{n+1} = (a + b x_n + g y_n)/(A + x_n), y_{n+1} = x_n, with nonnegative parameters and positive denominators, extend and generalize its period-two trichotomy to broader planar rational systems: when g < b + A every solution converges to a finite limit, when g = b + A every solution converges to a not necessarily prime period-two solution, and when g > b + A some initial conditions produce unbounded solutions. The problem is to identify analogous trichotomy statements and parameter regimes for rational systems in the plane.

accepted.question_text: For the seventeen positive-parameter planar rational systems singled out in Appendix 3, determine and prove the exact boundedness character of both components for all nonnegative initial conditions with positive denominators. Here B* means the corresponding component is conjectured to be bounded for every solution, and U* means the corresponding component is conjectured to be unbounded for some parameter values and initial conditions. The systems and conjectured component behaviors are: (12,31): x_{n+1}=a1/(x_n+y_n), y_{n+1}=(a2+x_n)/(A2+y_n), conjectured (B*,B*); (23,23): x_{n+1}=(a1+g1 y_n)/x_n, y_{n+1}=(a2+b2 x_n)/y_n, conjectured (U*,U*); (23,31): x_{n+1}=(a1+g1 y_n)/x_n, y_{n+1}=(a2+b2 x_n)/(1+y_n), conjectured (U*,U*); (23,34): x_{n+1}=(a1+g1 y_n)/x_n, y_{n+1}=(b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(1+y_n), conjectured (U*,U*); (23,35): x_{n+1}=(a1+g1 y_n)/x_n, y_{n+1}=(b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(1+x_n), conjectured (U*,B*); (23,46): x_{n+1}=(a1+g1 y_n)/x_n, y_{n+1}=(a2+b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(1+y_n), conjectured (U*,U*); (30,30): x_{n+1}=(a1+b1 x_n)/(B1 x_n+y_n), y_{n+1}=(a2+g2 y_n)/(B2 x_n+y_n), conjectured (B*,B*); (30,31): x_{n+1}=(a1+b1 x_n)/(B1 x_n+y_n), y_{n+1}=(a2+b2 x_n)/(A2+y_n), conjectured (B*,B*); (30,34): x_{n+1}=(a1+b1 x_n)/(B1 x_n+y_n), y_{n+1}=(b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(A2+y_n), conjectured (B*,B*); (31,31): x_{n+1}=(a1+g1 y_n)/(1+x_n), y_{n+1}=(a2+b2 x_n)/(1+y_n), conjectured (U*,U*); (31,34): x_{n+1}=(a1+g1 y_n)/(1+x_n), y_{n+1}=(b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(1+y_n), conjectured (U*,U*); (31,35): x_{n+1}=(a1+g1 y_n)/(1+x_n), y_{n+1}=(b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(A2+x_n), conjectured (B*,B*); (31,46): x_{n+1}=(a1+g1 y_n)/(1+x_n), y_{n+1}=(a2+b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(1+y_n), conjectured (U*,U*); (34,34): x_{n+1}=(b1 x_n+g1 y_n)/(1+x_n), y_{n+1}=(b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(1+y_n), conjectured (U*,U*); (34,46): x_{n+1}=(b1 x_n+g1 y_n)/(A1+x_n), y_{n+1}=(a2+b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(A2+y_n), conjectured (U*,U*); (34,47): x_{n+1}=(b1 x_n+g1 y_n)/(1+x_n), y_{n+1}=(a2+b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(A2+x_n), conjectured (B*,B*); and (46,46): x_{n+1}=(a1+b1 x_n+g1 y_n)/(1+x_n), y_{n+1}=(a2+b2 x_n+g2 y_n)/(1+y_n), conjectured (U*,U*).

accepted.question_text: For each of the 47 planar rational systems among the non-single-equation group of 300 special cases that may be competitive for some parameter ranges and are nowhere cooperative, determine whether the competitive-system monotonicity hypotheses corresponding to Theorem 3.12 or Theorem 3.13 hold, and then determine the global behavior of all solutions. The 47 systems are (14,l), (15,l), and (29,l) with l in {30,35,36,43,45,47,48,49}; (30,l) with l in {30,35,36,38,43,45,47,48,49}; (35,38), (35,43), (36,38), (36,43); and (38,l), (43,l) with l in {43,45,47,48,49}. The relevant Theorem 3.12 hypothesis is that a one-step simultaneous decrease or simultaneous increase of both components forces the same direction in the previous step, yielding eventual monotonicity of both component sequences; the relevant Theorem 3.13 hypothesis is the analogous two-step condition yielding eventual monotonicity of the four even and odd component subsequences.

accepted.question_text: For each of the 31 planar rational systems that may be cooperative in some parameter range and nowhere competitive, determine the exact parameter region where the system is cooperative, determine whether the cooperative-system monotonicity hypotheses corresponding to Theorem 3.16 or Theorem 3.17 are satisfied, and determine the global character of all solutions. The 31 systems are (35,40), (35,46), (36,40), (36,46), (45,46); (k,l) with k <= l, k in {34,46}, and l in {34,35,36,40,45,46,47,48,49}; and (k,l) with k <= l, k in {25,40}, and l in {34,35,36,45,46,47,48,49}. The relevant Theorem 3.16 hypothesis is a one-step mixed-direction monotonicity implication for cooperative systems, yielding eventual monotonicity of both component sequences; the relevant Theorem 3.17 hypothesis is the analogous two-step condition yielding eventual monotonicity of the four even and odd component subsequences.
